name: PRTF — Physical Red Team Framework
attribution: PRTF — Physical Red Team Framework, RedTeam.vip (https://redteam.vip/prtf/)
id_policy: Technique IDs are permanent and never reused.

tactics.name: Reconnaissance
tactics.description: The operator is gathering information about the site, its people and its security before going on site.

techniques.name: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT)
techniques.description: OSINT is the foundation of every engagement. Before you ever step foot near a target, you should understand the organization's physical footprint, employee structure, security posture, and daily rhythms — all from publicly available sources. This includes social media, job postings (which reveal security vendors, access control systems, and software in use), satellite imagery, LinkedIn profiles, corporate websites, and leaked data. The goal is to build a target dossier that informs pretext selection, identifies key personnel to impersonate or social engineer, and reveals potential physical vulnerabilities before any risk is assumed.

blue_team.detection: Unusual volume of employee LinkedIn lookups; Google Dorking patterns in web server logs; Shodan scans originating from non-customer IPs.
blue_team.countermeasures: Limit public exposure of org charts; use LinkedIn privacy settings for sensitive roles; monitor for Google dork patterns targeting your domain; configure Shodan monitoring alerts.

techniques.name: Aerial Reconnaissance
techniques.description: Drones provide a perspective on a target that is impossible to obtain from street level. A single aerial pass can reveal roof access points, fence lines, security camera placement, loading dock activity, parking lot patterns, and guard patrol routes. This intelligence directly informs entry planning and evasion strategy. FAA Part 107 certification is required for commercial operations, and flight planning must account for controlled airspace and LAANC authorization. Always fly within the scope of the engagement authorization.

blue_team.detection: Drone sighting by security personnel or cameras; unusual aircraft near facility perimeter.
blue_team.countermeasures: Deploy drone detection systems; train security staff to report drone sightings; visual barriers for sensitive roof areas.

techniques.name: Perimeter Surveying
techniques.description: On-foot walkthroughs of the target perimeter reveal details that no aerial or satellite imagery can capture — the exact type of door hardware on employee entrances, whether a badge reader is Wiegand or OSDP, which doors have REX sensors, where cameras have blind spots, and how employees behave at access points. Perimeter surveying should be conducted at multiple times of day and documented thoroughly. Body-worn cameras allow you to review footage later without raising suspicion during the walk.

blue_team.detection: Individual spending extended time near perimeter without apparent purpose; returning multiple times at different hours.
blue_team.countermeasures: Exterior cameras covering perimeter approaches; security patrol at irregular intervals; signage indicating surveillance.

techniques.name: Long-Range Photography
techniques.description: A high-zoom camera allows you to document target details from a safe standoff distance without raising suspicion. This is particularly valuable for capturing badge designs, access control hardware model numbers (which reveal bypass techniques), security camera models, and employee behavior around entry points. A polarized filter significantly reduces glare when shooting through glass or at reflective surfaces, and can reveal interior details like badge readers or reception desk layouts.

blue_team.detection: Individual with telephoto lens or spotting scope aimed at facility; unusual vehicle parked with line of sight to entry points or sensitive areas.
blue_team.countermeasures: Landscaping and physical barriers limiting line-of-sight to sensitive areas; frosted or one-way glass on ground-floor windows; awareness training for security staff to report suspicious surveillance.

techniques.name: Infrared / Low-Light Observation
techniques.description: Many security cameras and motion sensors use infrared illumination that is invisible to the naked eye but detectable with IR-capable optics. A handheld IR monocular allows you to map active IR illuminators and identify camera coverage in low-light environments without revealing your position. This is critical for planning after-hours or early-morning entries where IR-based motion detectors are the primary detection mechanism.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect — operator uses IR viewer passively; IR illuminator use detectable with IR-sensitive camera.
blue_team.countermeasures: IR-blocking window film on sensitive areas; conduct after-hours security walks to identify IR camera placements; use IR-opaque barriers around sensitive equipment.

techniques.name: Borescope Inspection
techniques.description: A borescope is a thin flexible camera that can be inserted into door gaps, under doors, through small openings, or into ceiling tile gaps to inspect spaces that are otherwise inaccessible. During recon, this tool reveals what lies on the other side of a door — whether a latch is exposed, whether a lever handle is present, or whether a REX sensor is positioned in a reachable location. It is also useful for inspecting the interior of access control enclosures.

blue_team.detection: Thin flexible cable visible at door gap during extended use; time at door without key; camera coverage of entry point.
blue_team.countermeasures: Door gap reduction via weatherstripping and proper thresholds; camera coverage of entry points from multiple angles; motion sensors on interior side of controlled doors.

techniques.name: Dumpster Diving
techniques.description: Discarded materials from a target organization can yield an extraordinary amount of intelligence — shredded documents, old ID badges, network diagrams, internal memos, access control system documentation, vendor invoices, and physical keys. Dumpster diving is legal in most US jurisdictions once waste has been placed for collection on public property, but always confirm scope with the client and consult local statutes. This technique often produces the most operationally valuable intelligence of any recon method.

blue_team.detection: Individual accessing dumpsters or recycling areas; unsecured documents in waste streams.
blue_team.countermeasures: Cross-cut or micro-cut shredding of all paper; locked waste containers; clean-desk policy.

techniques.name: Employee & Badge Profiling
techniques.description: Understanding how employees look, dress, move, and behave at a target is essential for convincing impersonation and tailgating. This includes identifying badge designs (color, logo placement, clip type, lanyard color), uniform styles for different roles, and how security personnel interact with visitors. LinkedIn and social media often reveal employee photos with visible badges or uniforms. Long-range photography during perimeter surveying supplements this with real-time behavioral data.

blue_team.detection: Individual observing employee entry/exit patterns; photographing badge designs or access hardware; loitering near entry points during shift changes.
blue_team.countermeasures: Camera coverage of all entry points; employee awareness training on credential exposure; challenge anyone photographing staff or access hardware; anti-skimming badge sleeves.

techniques.name: Wireless Network Discovery
techniques.description: Passive wireless scanning during recon reveals the target's network infrastructure without generating traffic or triggering alerts. This identifies SSIDs in use (which may reveal naming conventions, vendors, or segmentation), security protocols, the presence of guest networks, and potentially hidden SSIDs. A directional antenna allows selective scanning of specific areas or floors of a building. This intelligence feeds directly into wireless attack planning and rogue AP strategy.

blue_team.detection: Wireless scanning tools produce probe requests; unusual 802.11 probe patterns near perimeter; WIDS alerts.
blue_team.countermeasures: Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS); minimize SSID broadcast range; 5GHz-only networks.

techniques.name: RFID Frequency Identification
techniques.description: Before attempting to clone an access card, you must identify the frequency and protocol in use at the target's readers. Most commercial access control systems operate on 125kHz (HID Prox, EM4100) or 13.56MHz (HID iCLASS, MIFARE). An RFID field detector or diagnostics card identifies the frequency of any reader by simply presenting it — no credentials or cloning required. This single step determines which tools you need and whether cloning is feasible with your current kit.

blue_team.detection: Individual holding device near access readers without badging; repeated failed badge reads.
blue_team.countermeasures: Monitor access control logs for repeated failed reads; anti-skimming reader covers; OSDP encrypted readers.

techniques.name: Long-Range RFID Reading
techniques.description: Standard RFID readers have a read range of a few centimeters. Weaponized long-range readers extend this to several feet, enabling credential capture at a natural standoff distance — shaking someone's hand, standing behind them in line, or sitting nearby in a lobby. The captured data is then used to clone a credential for later replay. This technique requires careful scoping with the client, as it directly captures employee credentials.

blue_team.detection: Individual with directional antenna near entry points; unusual equipment near access readers.
blue_team.countermeasures: OSDP encrypted readers defeat Wiegand-based skimming; reader covers and shields; relocate readers away from exterior walls.

techniques.name: Team Communications Planning
techniques.description: Reliable out-of-band communications between team members is a critical operational requirement for any multi-operator physical engagement. Cell phones are vulnerable to network outages and RF shielding inside large buildings. Two-way radios provide direct, infrastructure-independent comms that function in basements, parking garages, and RF-shielded spaces. Establish brevity codes, challenge/response signals, and abort signals before every operation — not during.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect directly; encrypted comms leave no exploitable signal; unusual radio frequency activity near facility may be detectable.
blue_team.countermeasures: RF monitoring near sensitive facilities; detect unusual encrypted radio traffic; TSCM awareness for high-security sites.

techniques.name: Credential & Badge Observation
techniques.description: Visual capture of badge designs, access control hardware, and employee credential presentation behaviors during recon feeds directly into badge fabrication and impersonation. Key details to document include badge orientation, logo placement, color coding by department or clearance level, holographic elements, clip or lanyard type, and whether employees present badges to readers or use proximity. This documentation drives the social engineering and badge fabrication phases.

blue_team.detection: Individual observing or photographing badge readers and access hardware; camera aimed at entry points during badge use.
blue_team.countermeasures: Camera covers or shields on readers; awareness training on credential handling; anti-skimming covers; employees aware not to display badge faces unnecessarily.

tactics.name: Evasion
tactics.description: The operator is trying to avoid being seen, recorded or challenged while on site.

techniques.name: Camera Avoidance & Blind Spot Mapping
techniques.description: Physical security camera systems almost always have blind spots — angles, distances, or occlusions that limit their coverage. Mapping these during recon using aerial photography and perimeter surveys allows route planning that minimizes camera exposure. Understanding camera types (PTZ vs. fixed, analog vs. IP), field of view, and mounting height informs how much movement is safe and at what distances. Recon footage from a body-worn camera is ideal for post-survey blind spot analysis.

blue_team.detection: Behavioral analytics flagging movement patterns avoiding camera coverage; individual traversing unusual paths through facility.
blue_team.countermeasures: Eliminate camera blind spots through overlapping coverage design; use PTZ cameras for dynamic coverage; motion-triggered lighting in blind spots; regular camera coverage audits.

techniques.name: Behavioral Blending
techniques.description: The most reliable evasion technique is not avoiding cameras — it is not triggering a human response when seen on camera or in person. Moving at a purposeful, unhurried pace appropriate to the cover role, avoiding lingering or searching behaviors, maintaining appropriate eye contact with staff, and responding naturally to challenges are all components of behavioral blending. An operator who looks like they belong will be ignored even on recorded footage.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect in real time; post-incident review of footage may reveal operator; behavioral analytics on extended presence without purpose.
blue_team.countermeasures: Behavioral analytics systems; security staff training on anomalous behavior detection; challenge culture empowering staff to verify identity of anyone lingering without clear purpose.

techniques.name: Appearance Management
techniques.description: Clothing and equipment choices directly affect how personnel and security staff perceive an operator. Tactical clothing, multi-pocket vests, military-style gear, and anything that reads as 'security professional' draws attention in civilian environments. The target environment's dress code — identified during recon — should dictate attire. Hi-vis is paradoxically one of the most effective cover appearances in many environments because it signals 'authorized worker' without requiring further explanation.

blue_team.detection: Inconsistencies in attire relative to stated role; uniform not matching known vendor or contractor style; security staff challenge.
blue_team.countermeasures: Approved vendor uniform reference guide for security staff; challenge culture; all visitors required to present verifiable ID regardless of attire.

techniques.name: Counter-Surveillance Detection
techniques.description: A physical red team operator must be aware of the possibility that they are being watched — by security personnel, private investigators, or protective details. Surveillance detection routes (SDRs) are planned movement paths that create opportunities to identify surveillance through deliberate direction changes, pauses, and observation points. Identifying surveillance before it becomes interdiction allows an abort decision while the operational window is still open.

blue_team.detection: Virtually undetectable — operator is observing and moving normally; unusual stop-and-start movement patterns may appear in analytics.
blue_team.countermeasures: Irregular security patrol patterns make SDRs harder to execute; randomize guard routes; CCTV with behavioral analytics for extended loitering near facility.

techniques.name: Alarm System Awareness & Avoidance
techniques.description: Motion detectors, door contacts, glass break sensors, and PIR sensors are the primary electronic detection layer in most commercial facilities. Understanding sensor placement from recon, technology type, and coverage areas allows route planning that minimizes alarm activation. Most PIR sensors have a reset time after activation that can be exploited for movement timing. Identifying alarm system vendors during recon allows research of known sensor blind spots.

tools.name: Motion sensor detection via IR monocular

blue_team.detection: Alarm activation if evasion fails; unusual tampering with sensor housings; motion near sensors without activation.
blue_team.countermeasures: Dual-technology sensors (PIR + microwave); tamper-evident sensor housings; supervised alarm zones that alert on sensor disconnection.

techniques.name: Sensor Defeat
techniques.description: When sensor avoidance is not possible, active defeat techniques can suppress alarm activation. REX sensors can be triggered intentionally to hold a door lock released. Solenoid-based sensors may respond to magnetic interference. PIR sensors can sometimes be defeated by moving very slowly or by thermal masking. Each technique requires specific knowledge of the sensor type and must be validated against the exact variant encountered.

blue_team.detection: Alarm activation if defeat attempt fails; tampering with sensor housing detectable during inspection; motion near sensors without activation may indicate defeat.
blue_team.countermeasures: Dual-technology sensors (PIR + microwave) cannot be defeated with static objects; tamper-evident sensor housings; supervised alarm zones alerting on sensor disconnection; regular sensor testing.

techniques.name: Covert Carry
techniques.description: Carrying physical access tools covertly requires attention to both concealment and detectability. Standard steel picks are ferromagnetic and will trigger metal detector portals and handheld wand searches. Titanium picks are non-ferrous and do not trigger standard magnetic metal detection. The covert pocket belt provides a concealed carry option for pick sets that passes casual visual inspection. Equipment loadout should be calibrated to the expected security screening environment for each engagement.

blue_team.detection: Metal detector or X-ray screening may detect ferrous tools; visual inspection may reveal tool outlines; non-ferrous picks pass metal detectors.
blue_team.countermeasures: Metal detector portals and wand screening at entry; X-ray of bags and equipment; pat-down for high-security areas; non-ferrous picks (titanium, aluminum) bypass metal detection — physical pat-down required.

techniques.name: IR & Low-Light Awareness
techniques.description: Active IR illuminators used by security cameras are invisible to the naked eye but detectable with any IR-sensitive camera or monocular. Knowing which cameras are IR-enabled and the radius of their IR illumination allows an operator to avoid areas where they would be visible on IR-enhanced footage even in apparent darkness. An infrared monocular during pre-entry assessment reveals the full IR illumination map of the approach path.

blue_team.detection: IR illuminator detection requires IR-sensitive camera; operator using IR viewer is not visible to the naked eye.
blue_team.countermeasures: Regular camera maintenance ensuring IR illuminators function; conduct nighttime security walks; IR-opaque barriers for sensitive equipment and areas.

techniques.name: Digital & OPSEC Footprint Minimization
techniques.description: Every device an operator carries creates a digital signature — phone location data, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi probe requests, IMSI exposure to cell towers, and biometric identifiers in access logs. Minimizing this footprint requires leaving personal devices behind, using burner hardware, disabling unnecessary wireless interfaces, and planning movement that does not create a traceable digital record. OPSEC discipline before, during, and after an engagement is what separates a clean exit from a post-incident attribution finding.

tools.name: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi disabled when not in use

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect directly; combined with other techniques, digital footprint minimization makes post-incident attribution harder.
blue_team.countermeasures: Cellular IMSI catchers can detect unusual device behavior; Bluetooth scanning logs at entry points; require visitor device registration; deploy wireless monitoring throughout facility.

tactics.name: Lockpicking
tactics.description: The operator is trying to open a mechanical lock without its key, leaving it working.

techniques.name: Single Pin Picking (SPP)
techniques.description: SPP involves applying light rotational tension to the cylinder with a tension wrench while using a hook pick to lift each pin stack individually to the shear line. Manufacturing tolerances cause pins to bind sequentially, allowing each pin to be set one at a time until the cylinder rotates. SPP is slower than raking but more reliable on quality locks and leaves fewer marks than raking or bumping. It is the primary technique for locks that require precise, quiet manipulation.
prerequisites: Pin tumbler cylinder confirmed at target

blue_team.detection: Scratches around keyway; time spent at locked door without key use; picking sounds in quiet environments.
blue_team.countermeasures: High-security cylinders (Medeco, Mul-T-Lock, Abloy) are pick-resistant; security pins increase difficulty; door alarms triggered by extended manipulation.

techniques.name: Raking
techniques.description: Raking uses a serrated or wavy pick moved rapidly back and forth under light tension to randomly set multiple pins simultaneously. It is faster than SPP but less reliable on quality locks. Raking is the preferred opening move when speed matters more than precision — entry points with low-grade cylinders (common in commercial and institutional settings) often open within seconds. It is typically the first technique attempted on any unknown lock before committing to SPP.

blue_team.detection: Scratching around keyway; time at door without key; more visible tool manipulation than SPP.
blue_team.countermeasures: Security pins make raking significantly less effective; high-security cylinders; access log monitoring.

techniques.name: Dimple Lock Picking
techniques.description: Dimple locks use a key with cuts on its face rather than its edge, requiring a different pick geometry. They are common in higher-security residential and commercial applications in Europe and increasingly in North America. Dedicated dimple picks navigate the lock's unique geometry, and tension is applied in a different plane than standard pin tumbler picking. Encountering a dimple lock on target requires specific tooling — standard picks will not engage the mechanism.
prerequisites: Dimple lock confirmed (key cuts on face, not edge)

blue_team.detection: Time at door without key; specialized pick visible in keyway; scratching on face of cylinder.
blue_team.countermeasures: High-security dimple cylinders with security pins; limited availability of quality dimple picks reduces casual attack risk; door alarms.

techniques.name: Tubular Lock Picking
techniques.description: Tubular locks have pins arranged in a circular pattern around the key's axis and are found on vending machines, bike locks, display cases, and some alarm panels. Tubular pick tools simultaneously tension all pins and allow the operator to set each one by feel. Many tubular locks are low-security and open quickly with the right tool. A tubular lockpick is a niche but essential addition to any red team kit for targets with display cases, server cage locks, or vending equipment.
prerequisites: Tubular lock confirmed at target (vending machine, bike lock, alarm panel)

blue_team.detection: Specialized tool visible at tubular keyway; time at target lock.
blue_team.countermeasures: Upgrade vending machines and alarm panels to electronic access; high-security tubular cylinders; physical access control to areas containing tubular-locked equipment.

techniques.name: Disk Detainer Picking
techniques.description: Disk detainer locks use rotating disks rather than pin stacks and are common in medium-to-high security padlocks and some deadbolts. Dedicated disk detainer picks rotate each disk individually to the correct position while applying rotational tension. These locks require a completely different technique and tool set from pin tumbler picking and represent a meaningful skill investment beyond the core picking curriculum.
prerequisites: Disk detainer lock confirmed (typically medium-security padlocks, bike locks)

blue_team.detection: Specialized pick visible at disk detainer keyway; time at lock.
blue_team.countermeasures: High-security disk detainer cylinders; limited availability of quality picks reduces risk; use electronic access for high-security applications instead of disk detainer locks.

techniques.name: Wafer Lock Picking
techniques.description: Wafer locks are common in filing cabinets, desk drawers, interior doors, and low-security padlocks. They use flat wafers instead of pin stacks and are generally less secure than pin tumbler locks. Wafer pick sets navigate the wafer geometry and open most of these locks quickly. File cabinets and desk drawers at a target often contain the highest-value intelligence — credentials, access documentation, physical keys — making this technique disproportionately valuable relative to the minimal effort required.
prerequisites: Wafer lock confirmed (filing cabinet, desk drawer, interior door, low-security padlock)

blue_team.detection: Time at cabinet or furniture lock without key; pick tool visible in keyway; lock opened without authorized key.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace wafer lock furniture with electronic access or high-security pin tumbler locks for sensitive storage; key control policy; camera coverage of sensitive storage areas.

techniques.name: Warded Lock Picking
techniques.description: Warded locks are an older design found in padlocks, old door hardware, and some storage facilities. They have static internal obstacles (wards) that a key's profile must clear. Warded picks are designed with minimal profiles to bypass these wards without the correct key shape. Most warded locks have minimal security against picking and open with negligible effort once the correct pick profile is identified.
prerequisites: Warded lock confirmed (older padlock, storage hardware, antique door hardware)

blue_team.detection: Warded locks are legacy hardware — their presence is itself a vulnerability indicator.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace all warded locks with modern pin tumbler or electronic access; warded locks provide minimal security and should not be used in any security application.

techniques.name: Combination Lock Decoding
techniques.description: Combination locks can be defeated without picking by decoding — determining the combination through feel, measurement, or manipulation of internal contact points. Systematic decoders work through combinations by feel or measurement. Some locks have design weaknesses that allow the combination to be read with minimal effort. Many cheap combination padlocks protecting file rooms and storage areas can be decoded in under a minute, and even higher-quality dial locks have well-documented decoding procedures.
prerequisites: Ability to apply controlled tension to shackle

blue_team.detection: Time spent at combination lock without opening; manipulation under tension may leave wear marks on dial.
blue_team.countermeasures: High-security combination locks (Sergeant & Greenleaf, Sargent & Greenleaf); combination change policy; electronic access preferred over combination locks for security applications.

techniques.name: Bump Keys
techniques.description: A bump key is a specially cut key that, when struck while applying light rotational tension, momentarily bounces all pin stacks above the shear line simultaneously — opening the lock. Bump keys must match the target lock's keyway profile. The technique is fast and requires minimal skill but is audible and leaves visible marks on the keyway. Best used when speed outweighs stealth, or when the target environment's ambient noise floor makes the strike unremarkable.
prerequisites: Bump-resistant cylinder NOT present (Medeco, Mul-T-Lock, Abloy are immune)

blue_team.detection: Audible impact sound; scratching on keyway; time at door without key use.
blue_team.countermeasures: Bump-resistant cylinders (Medeco, Abloy, Mul-T-Lock) are immune; anti-bump security pins; access control logs for off-hours access.

techniques.name: Plug Spinner
techniques.description: After picking a lock in the wrong rotational direction, a plug spinner rapidly spins the cylinder back past the set position to the opposite direction without dropping the set pins. This avoids the need to re-pick the lock when tension was applied in the wrong direction — a common occurrence when the correct rotation is unknown before picking. A plug spinner is a small but meaningful time-saver on harder cylinders where re-picking costs significant effort.

blue_team.detection: Indicates lock picking has already occurred; audible spinning if detected.
blue_team.countermeasures: High-security cylinders reduce picking success that would necessitate plug spinner; door alarms; access log monitoring.

techniques.name: Lishi Tools (decode + pick)
techniques.description: Lishi tools are specialized 2-in-1 instruments that simultaneously pick and decode a lock cylinder — revealing the key's bitting while opening the lock. Originally designed for automotive locksmiths, they are widely used in physical red teaming. A Lishi tool opens the lock and returns the full key code as a byproduct, enabling key duplication for persistent re-entry. They are keyway-specific, so engagement planning must account for which Lishi profiles match the target's hardware.
prerequisites: Pin tumbler cylinder with accessible keyway

blue_team.detection: Tool profile visible in keyway; time at door; decoded bitting can enable key duplication.
blue_team.countermeasures: Restricted/patented keyways prevent unauthorized duplication; key control policies and audit logs; high-security cylinders.

techniques.name: EDC Picks (non-ferrous)
techniques.description: Standard steel picks are ferromagnetic and will trigger metal detector portals and handheld wand searches. Titanium and G10 composite picks are non-ferrous and do not trigger standard magnetic metal detection, making them suitable for EDC in environments where screening may be encountered. Note that advanced security screening — millimeter wave, X-ray, or high-sensitivity detectors — may still detect picks based on shape or density. No EDC pick set should be considered universally undetectable.

blue_team.detection: Non-ferrous picks do not trigger metal detectors; visual inspection or X-ray required for detection.
blue_team.countermeasures: X-ray screening of bags; pat-down required for high-security areas; metal detectors alone are insufficient — non-ferrous picks are specifically designed to bypass them.

tactics.name: Bypass
tactics.description: The operator is trying to defeat a door, latch or lock without picking it.

techniques.name: Latch Slipping
techniques.description: Many spring latches can be slipped back into the door using a thin shim inserted into the door gap, bypassing the lock entirely. The Jim tool and Mica shims are designed for this purpose. The technique is effective on doors where the latch is exposed in the frame gap — a common condition in commercial buildings where door frames are misaligned or where the strike plate does not fully cover the latch bolt. This is one of the most frequently successful bypass techniques in real engagements.

blue_team.detection: Door open alert if door state is monitored; physical evidence of latch damage or shim marks on door edge; camera footage of entry.
blue_team.countermeasures: Deadbolt required alongside spring latch for all exterior doors; door position sensors tied to alarm; anti-shimming latch guards; door gap reduction via proper frame installation.

techniques.name: Over-Door / Film Attack
techniques.description: Camera film or a thin loop of material inserted over the top of a door and into the frame gap can be used to manipulate levers, thumb turns, or latches on the interior side. The technique is effective on outward-opening doors where interior hardware is accessible through the door gap. RTT's camera film is specifically designed for this application and is one of the most covert bypass tools available — there is no audible indication of the attack and it leaves no visible marks.
prerequisites: Over-door gap accessible — door not sealed at top

blue_team.detection: Time at door; film loop visible above door if observed from inside; door open alert.
blue_team.countermeasures: Door top seals reducing gap; door alarms; camera coverage of door from inside showing top of frame; door frame reinforcement.

techniques.name: Under-Door Tool (UDT)
techniques.description: The under-door tool is inserted under the door gap and manipulates a lever handle or thumb turn on the interior side from outside the door. It is highly effective on lever-handle doors with interior egress hardware and is one of the most reliable bypass techniques against commercial lever hardware. The tool requires approximately 1cm of clearance under the door and works on a wide range of commercial configurations. An air wedge can supplement clearance on tighter doors.
prerequisites: Interior lever handle or thumb turn confirmed

blue_team.detection: Door open alert if door state monitored; camera coverage of entry point; marks under door from tool.
blue_team.countermeasures: Door bottom seals reducing clearance below 1cm; door alarms on all access-controlled doors; camera coverage of entry points from angles showing under-door approach.

techniques.name: Crash Bar / Double Door Tool (DDT)
techniques.description: Double doors with crash bars (panic hardware) often have a gap between the two door leafs that can be exploited. The DDT is inserted into this gap to depress the crash bar or manipulate the latch from outside. This technique bypasses the deadbolt or cylinder entirely on many commercial double-door configurations and is particularly effective on secondary entry points like emergency exits and stairwell doors where double-door panic hardware is standard.
prerequisites: Double door with crash bar confirmed

blue_team.detection: Tool visible between door leafs; door open alert; camera footage of exterior approach.
blue_team.countermeasures: Door edge guards reducing gap between leafs; door alarms; camera coverage; astragal (overlapping door edge) prevents access to gap.

techniques.name: J-Tool (thumb-turn bypass)
techniques.description: The J-tool is a long, flexible instrument inserted through the door gap — typically augmented by an air wedge — to reach and rotate a thumb-turn lock on the interior side. It is effective on doors with sufficient frame clearance and works on a wide range of residential and light commercial thumb-turn configurations. A staple for hotel corridors, apartment buildings, and older commercial doors where thumb-turn deadbolts are used without additional security hardware.

blue_team.detection: Tool visible through door gap; door open alert; camera footage.
blue_team.countermeasures: Door bottom and side seals minimizing gap; thumb turn guards; door alarms; double-cylinder deadbolts (keyed both sides) prevent thumb-turn bypass.

techniques.name: Traveler's Hook
techniques.description: The Traveler's Hook is a compact, low-profile tool designed to manipulate latches that have a small amount of travel or gap exposure. It is effective on doors where the latch can be partially accessed through the door gap and is a fast, covert option for initial latch bypass on lighter commercial hardware. Its small form factor makes it an ideal EDC bypass tool when profile and weight are priorities.

blue_team.detection: Time at door with tool; door open alert; camera footage.
blue_team.countermeasures: Latch guards preventing access to latch bolt; door alarms; anti-shimming latch bolts; camera coverage of entry points.

techniques.name: Adams Rite Bypass
techniques.description: Adams Rite is a common latch mechanism used on aluminum storefront doors — the glass-framed commercial doors found throughout retail, office, and institutional buildings. The latch can be bypassed using a specialized hook tool or driver that manipulates the latch bolt directly through the narrow gap in the face plate. This technique is extremely common on commercial targets and any operator working corporate or retail environments should be fluent with it.

blue_team.detection: Door alarm on state change; camera footage; aluminum storefront doors are high-risk.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace Adams Rite latches with deadlatch versions; add secondary locking; door alarms; camera coverage of storefront entry points.

techniques.name: Air Wedge / Door Frame Separation
techniques.description: An air wedge is inserted into a door gap and slowly inflated to widen the gap between the door and frame. This creates access for other bypass tools — J-tool, film attack, UDT — that require more clearance than the natural door gap provides. Air wedges are low-noise, non-destructive, and compatible with most commercial door frames. They are a force multiplier for the rest of the latch and door hardware bypass toolkit.

blue_team.detection: Audible air pumping sound; visible frame distortion; door open alert if monitored; camera footage of approach.
blue_team.countermeasures: Reinforced door frames and strike plates; door alarms on all access-controlled doors; anti-spread door hardware; camera coverage of all entry points.

techniques.name: Slip Jim / SeaRAT
techniques.description: The Slip Jim is a thin, flexible tool used for rapid latch access on doors with exposed latch bolts. It can slip behind a latch bolt and retract it directly without any tension or picking. Effective on light commercial and residential latches where the bolt is not fully recessed into a strike plate, and particularly useful on interior doors within a facility once initial perimeter access has been achieved.

blue_team.detection: Tool insertion visible; door open alert; camera footage of exterior approach.
blue_team.countermeasures: Anti-shimming latch bolts; latch guards; door alarms; camera coverage; spring latch replacement with deadbolt.

techniques.name: Padlock Shim Attack
techniques.description: Padlock shims are thin aluminum inserts pushed into the shackle slot of a padlock, releasing the shackle without a key or picking. The shim depresses the locking pawl that holds the shackle in place. Most single-locking padlocks are vulnerable; double-locking padlocks require two shims inserted simultaneously. Shims are disposable, fast, and require no skill — making them one of the highest return-on-investment bypass tools for anyone regularly encountering padlocked gates, cages, or equipment rooms.
prerequisites: Open-shackle padlock confirmed (not shrouded or protected shackle)

blue_team.detection: Shim visible in shackle slot; padlock opens without key; camera coverage of padlock location.
blue_team.countermeasures: Shrouded shackle padlocks prevent shim access; use closed-shackle padlocks for high-security applications; lock boxes or hasps protecting shackle.

techniques.name: American Padlock Bypass Driver
techniques.description: Several American Lock series padlocks have a design vulnerability where a shaped driver inserted into the keyway and pressed against the locking mechanism releases the shackle without picking. This is a direct bypass of the lock mechanism and is significantly faster than picking. American Lock padlocks are extremely common on utility gates, HVAC equipment enclosures, and dumpster areas at commercial targets.
prerequisites: American Lock Series 700 or 1100 confirmed (not Series 5 or solid-body)

blue_team.detection: Padlock opens without key; driver tool visible; camera footage.
blue_team.countermeasures: Upgrade to Series 5 or solid-body American padlocks not affected by bypass; shrouded shackle padlocks; electronic locks for high-security applications.

techniques.name: Comb Pick (padlock bypass)
techniques.description: A comb pick is designed specifically for spring-loaded padlocks. Its toothed profile simultaneously depresses all spring-loaded pins in the lock, allowing the shackle to release. It is a direct mechanical bypass rather than a picking technique and works without any skill or feedback. Most cheap padlocks used on storage cages, utility rooms, and equipment cabinets are vulnerable to this approach.

blue_team.detection: Padlock opens without key; comb pick tool visible; camera footage.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace spring-loaded padlocks with pin tumbler or disc detainer padlocks; use closed-shackle or shrouded designs; electronic access for high-security applications.

techniques.name: Jiggler Keys (cabinet / furniture)
techniques.description: Jiggler keys are a set of generic try keys with varied cut profiles designed for wafer-lock furniture, cabinets, desk drawers, and low-security padlocks. They are rocked and jiggled in the keyway while light tension is applied, mimicking the action of the correct key. File cabinet jigglers are particularly valuable on engagements where office floor access has been achieved and a file cabinet warrants attention.

blue_team.detection: Key insertion and manipulation at cabinet lock; time at cabinet; camera coverage of area.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace wafer lock furniture with electronic access or high-security pin tumbler locks; sensitive documents in security containers with restricted key access.

techniques.name: REX Sensor Triggering
techniques.description: Request-to-Exit sensors are positioned on the interior side of access-controlled doors and automatically release the electric lock when someone approaches from inside. Modern dual-technology REX sensors combine PIR with microwave or ultrasonic detection — these are significantly harder to defeat with static objects and should be confirmed as single-tech before attempting defeat. Many can be triggered from the exterior by inserting a thin nozzle through the door gap and directing a burst of compressed air at the sensor. The RTT REX Blaster is specifically designed for this application. This technique bypasses the entire access control system without any credential, picking, or electronic attack.
prerequisites: Single-technology PIR REX sensor confirmed (not dual-tech)

blue_team.detection: Access control log shows door open without valid credential read; camera footage of exterior showing tool or foreign object near door.
blue_team.countermeasures: Dual-technology REX sensors (PIR + microwave) cannot be defeated with static objects; configure access control to alert on door open without credential read; camera coverage of REX side.

techniques.name: Solenoid Manipulation
techniques.description: Many electric locks use a solenoid to hold the bolt in the locked position. A strong neodymium magnet placed against the door surface near the solenoid can interact with the magnetic field of the mechanism, potentially releasing the lock. Effectiveness is highly dependent on door construction, solenoid type, and magnet strength and position. Works best on lighter electric strike assemblies where the solenoid is close to the door surface.
prerequisites: Fail-safe electric lock confirmed (locked when powered, not fail-secure)
Lock body accessible through door gap or thin wall

blue_team.detection: Access control log shows door open without credential; video shows magnet application; fail-secure locks are completely immune.
blue_team.countermeasures: Use fail-secure locks (locked when power is removed) instead of fail-safe on high-security doors; magnetic shielding in lock body; access control alerts on door open without credential.

techniques.name: Keyed-Alike Service Keys
techniques.description: Many commercial and institutional properties use keyed-alike master key systems from major manufacturers for utility rooms, electrical panels, elevators, and mechanical spaces. Hooligan Keys produces a set of commonly used service keys that work on these keyed-alike locks across many unrelated properties. Carrying the appropriate service key for a target's building type can open mechanical rooms, utility corridors, and rooftop access doors without any bypass or picking.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect — operator presents a legitimate-looking key; access logs show valid access with no anomaly.
blue_team.countermeasures: Avoid keyed-alike systems from commodity vendors; use restricted or patented keyways; key control and audit procedures; prefer electronic access for high-security areas.

techniques.name: Panel & Cabinet Keys
techniques.description: Electrical panels, data cabinets, fire alarm control panels, and HVAC control boxes throughout commercial buildings typically use a small set of common key types — CH751, CH501, 1284X, and similar — that open the majority of utility boxes across many manufacturers. Carrying an assortment of panel and cabinet keys provides access to network infrastructure, building systems, and physical security hardware in a wide range of commercial environments.

blue_team.detection: Individual accessing utility panels without clear authorization; key in use that matches generic panel key profile.
blue_team.countermeasures: Replace keyed-alike panel hardware with unique locks or electronic access; restrict panel key distribution; audit who holds master keys; monitor utility panel access with cameras.

techniques.name: Elevator & Fire Service Keys
techniques.description: Fire service elevator keys are standardized by jurisdiction and allow operation of elevators in emergency mode, bypassing normal call controls. In many buildings these same keys also access fire alarm panels, sprinkler rooms, and other life-safety infrastructure. The Sparrows Elevator Key Set covers the most common fire service key profiles in use across North America.

blue_team.detection: Individual using fire service key outside emergency context; elevator in service mode without maintenance visit scheduled.
blue_team.countermeasures: Log all fire service key use; coordinate with building management on scheduled maintenance; camera coverage of elevator service panels; physical key audit.

techniques.name: Hinge Pin Removal
techniques.description: On outward-opening doors where hinge pins are accessible from the exterior, removing the pins allows the door to be swung open from the hinge side regardless of lock state. This is an effective bypass on many exterior doors in older commercial and institutional buildings where hinges were not designed with security in mind. The CI hammerless hinge pin tool allows pin removal without striking tools that would create noise or visible damage.

blue_team.detection: Audible hammering during attack; hinge pins missing post-incident; camera coverage of hinge side.
blue_team.countermeasures: Security hinges with non-removable pins or set screws; hinge bolts (security studs); outward-opening doors avoided on high-security areas.

techniques.name: Fence Climbing
techniques.description: Perimeter fencing is a primary physical barrier on many targets. The RTT Folding Fence Climbers are lightweight aids that hook over a chain-link fence and provide a stable foothold for climbing without the grip and balance demands of unassisted climbing. They fold flat for covert carry and are particularly useful for targets where the fence line is the primary perimeter control. Fence line reconnaissance during PRTF-1 directly informs where climbing is most effective.

blue_team.detection: Highly visible — individual with climbing equipment near perimeter; camera footage; neighbor or patrol sighting.
blue_team.countermeasures: Anti-climb fence toppers (rotating spikes, added height); CCTV coverage of full perimeter; motion-triggered lighting; irregular patrol covering perimeter; vibration sensors on fence line.

techniques.name: Ladder-Assisted Elevated Access
techniques.description: Access points above ground level — second-floor windows, roof hatches, elevated loading docks, mechanical rooms — may be accessible via ladder when ground-level entry points are hardened. A telescoping ladder is compact enough to transport covertly and can be deployed quickly against a building exterior. Elevated access opens roof-level opportunities for implant placement, antenna installation, and HVAC duct access.

blue_team.detection: Highly visible — individual with ladder near building exterior; camera footage; neighbor or passerby reports.
blue_team.countermeasures: Camera coverage of building exterior including elevated access points; anti-climb features on drainpipes and facades; motion-triggered lighting; patrol checking perimeter including elevated areas.

techniques.name: Soft Barrier Defeat
techniques.description: Barbed wire, razor wire, and concertina wire are common perimeter barrier toppers that can be defeated non-destructively by placing a thick material over the wire to protect against cuts. A wool blanket is the most practical tool for this — cheap, widely available, and providing adequate protection against standard barbed wire. Used in conjunction with fence climbing on perimeter assessments where wire topping is present.

blue_team.detection: Physical evidence — cut or pressed-down wire; camera footage of perimeter crossing; patrol discovery.
blue_team.countermeasures: Anti-climb covers making wire defeat harder; CCTV coverage of perimeter; patrol at irregular intervals; vibration sensors on fence line; razor wire combined with solid barrier below.

tactics.name: Wireless & RF
tactics.description: The operator is trying to exploit Wi-Fi, RFID access credentials and other radio systems.

techniques.name: Evil Twin / Rogue AP
techniques.description: An evil twin attack creates a wireless access point that mimics a legitimate network, tricking clients into connecting to the attacker's infrastructure. Once connected, traffic can be intercepted, credentials harvested, and clients served malicious content. The Wi-Fi Pineapple automates much of this attack surface and is the standard tool for this technique. The Enterprise version is recommended for walkthrough assessments in large multi-floor environments due to its superior range.

blue_team.detection: WIDS detects rogue AP or evil twin inside facility; clients connecting to unknown BSSID; endpoint alert on connection to unrecognized network.
blue_team.countermeasures: WPA3 Enterprise with certificate-based authentication; WIDS deployed inside facility; 802.1X preventing credential capture from wireless; network segmentation limiting blast radius of captured credentials.

techniques.name: Passive Capture / Handshake Collection
techniques.description: Passive wireless capture involves monitoring 802.11 traffic without transmitting, collecting WPA2/WPA3 handshakes for offline cracking. The Pwnagotchi automates this as a standalone device — it moves through an area, captures handshakes, and logs them for later processing. This technique generates no transmission and is essentially invisible to wireless intrusion detection systems.

blue_team.detection: WIDS may detect passive scanning; WPA3 networks prevent handshake capture entirely; unusual probe requests near perimeter.
blue_team.countermeasures: Upgrade to WPA3 — handshakes not capturable; WIDS deployment; minimize signal leakage outside building; 802.1X for enterprise networks.

techniques.name: Long-Range Wi-Fi
techniques.description: A directional antenna dramatically extends the range at which Wi-Fi attacks can be conducted — from tens of meters to several hundred meters depending on antenna gain and environment. A cantenna is a DIY directional antenna built from a cylindrical metal can. This technique allows engagement of a target's wireless network from a parked vehicle or neighboring property, well outside the physical perimeter.

blue_team.detection: Unusual high-gain antenna visible near facility; WIDS may detect strong signal source from outside normal range; evil twin or passive capture session visible in wireless logs.
blue_team.countermeasures: Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS); minimize signal leakage outside building; 5GHz preferred for shorter range; 802.1X preventing credential capture.

techniques.name: Compact Wi-Fi Operations (EDC)
techniques.description: The Wi-Fi Pager is Hak5's compact Wi-Fi attack platform designed for covert carry and extended autonomous operation. Small enough to conceal in a pocket or bag, it can be deployed as a passive capture device, rogue AP, or drop implant in space-constrained environments where the full Pineapple is impractical. It is the EDC option for wireless attacks.

blue_team.detection: WIDS detects rogue AP or unusual probe patterns; compact device may be detected during physical search.
blue_team.countermeasures: WIDS with rogue AP detection; 802.1X on enterprise wireless; X-ray or physical search of bags at entry; NAC preventing unauthorized network access.

techniques.name: Internal Wireless Reconnaissance
techniques.description: Active and passive wireless reconnaissance conducted inside the target after initial access maps internal networks not visible from the perimeter. This includes identifying all SSIDs, BSSID mapping to physical locations, signal strength surveys, and identifying client devices. Conducting this inside the facility reveals internal networks, IoT segments, and management VLANs that support implant placement planning.

blue_team.detection: WIDS detects scanning activity inside facility; probe requests from unknown device; DHCP logs show unknown MAC address.
blue_team.countermeasures: WIDS deployed inside facility; 802.1X on all wireless; NAC; monitor DHCP logs for unknown devices; segment internal wireless networks.

techniques.name: Low-Frequency RFID Cloning
techniques.description: 125kHz RFID systems — HID Prox, EM4100, HID H10301 — are the most common access control technology in commercial buildings and one of the most vulnerable. Low-frequency credentials can typically be cloned in seconds using a Proxmark3 or Flipper Zero. The cloned credential is written to a T5577 emulation card or RFID bracelet and replayed at the target reader. LF cloning requires only a few seconds of proximity to the target card.
prerequisites: HID Prox, EM4100, or HID H10301 protocol identified

blue_team.detection: Credential used at unusual time or location; cloned credential used simultaneously with original; anti-passback violation.
blue_team.countermeasures: Migrate to 13.56MHz HF or OSDP-encrypted systems; anti-skimming card sleeves; monitor access logs for duplicate concurrent credential use.

techniques.name: High-Frequency / NFC Cloning
techniques.description: 13.56MHz systems — HID iCLASS, MIFARE Classic, DESFire, LEGIC — are more complex than LF. MIFARE Classic is vulnerable to well-documented attacks (Darkside, Nested). iCLASS SE and DESFire EV2 are significantly more resistant. The Proxmark3 is the primary tool for HF RFID analysis and cloning attempts, with Chameleon Ultra used for emulation and replay. This area requires understanding the target protocol before selecting an attack approach.
prerequisites: MIFARE Classic or iCLASS Legacy confirmed
DESFire EV2/EV3 NOT in use (requires reader implant instead)

blue_team.detection: Cloned credential used at unusual time or location; simultaneous use of same credential; anti-passback violation.
blue_team.countermeasures: Deploy DESFire EV2/EV3 with AES-128 — not clonable with current tools; OSDP encrypted readers; anti-passback rules; monitor for simultaneous credential use.

techniques.name: Long-Range RFID Skimming
techniques.description: In the active engagement phase, the same weaponized reader hardware deployed during recon is used to harvest credentials from employees in the target environment — lobbies, parking garages, elevators — for immediate replay. The operator carries the concealed reader in a bag or backpack and moves through high-traffic areas to collect credentials without any interaction. See PRTF-1.11 for the recon-phase application of this technique.

blue_team.detection: Individual with unusual equipment near entry points; reader logs showing credential read without badge presentation; OSDP tamper alert.
blue_team.countermeasures: OSDP encrypted readers prevent Wiegand-based skimming; anti-skimming reader covers; monitor for credential reads without associated door event; relocate readers from exterior walls.

techniques.name: RFID Emulation & Replay
techniques.description: After cloning a target credential, the data must be replayed at the access control reader. Emulation devices store the captured credential and present it electronically, simulating the target card. The Chameleon Ultra is purpose-built for this, can store multiple credentials, and can be configured to emulate specific card types. The RFID bracelet is a low-profile wearable option for hands-free proximity-based replay during social engineering approaches.

blue_team.detection: Cloned credential used at unusual time or location; anti-passback violation; simultaneous use of same credential at different readers.
blue_team.countermeasures: Anti-passback rules; credential geofencing; OSDP encrypted readers preventing credential replay; monitor for simultaneous credential use.

techniques.name: Access Control Reader Implant
techniques.description: Rather than cloning a single credential, a reader implant is placed on or behind an access control reader to harvest all credentials presented to it over time. The ESPKey taps the Wiegand data line between the reader and the control panel, capturing every card number presented. The Doppelganger board offers a more flexible platform for custom capture and relay scenarios. These implants provide a full credential harvest over the engagement window.
prerequisites: Access to rear of reader or cable run
Wiegand bus confirmed (OSDP encrypted NOT in use)
Power available from Wiegand bus (12V line)

blue_team.detection: Physical device discovery during security sweep; network anomaly from implant; WIDS detection; unusual RF emissions.
blue_team.countermeasures: Regular physical security sweeps (RF, visual); TSCM (Technical Surveillance Countermeasures) for high-security areas; NAC preventing implant network access; WIDS for wireless implants; audit all network ports regularly.

techniques.name: Sub-GHz Signal Capture & Replay
techniques.description: Sub-GHz signals (300–900MHz) are used by garage door openers, gate controllers, wireless key fobs, wireless alarm sensors, and remote access systems. The Flipper Zero can receive, record, and replay these signals, potentially opening gates, barriers, and doors using fixed-code systems. Rolling code systems require more sophisticated attacks. Sub-GHz reconnaissance during the perimeter survey phase often reveals entry vectors not discoverable by other means.
prerequisites: Static-code system confirmed OR RollJam setup prepared for rolling-code

references.title: RollJam — Universal Wireless Key Fob Attack
references.author: Samy Kamkar — DEF CON 23 (2015)

blue_team.detection: Replay of static-code signal triggers unintended door or gate open; RF monitoring detects capture devices near entry points.
blue_team.countermeasures: Rolling-code systems mandatory for all external gates; encrypted sub-GHz protocols where available; RF monitoring near sensitive entry points.

techniques.name: Infrared Signal Capture & Replay
techniques.description: Many building systems use IR remote controls — presentation room AV equipment, HVAC panels, entry intercoms, and some locking systems. The Flipper Zero captures and replays IR signals, allowing an operator to control building systems, disable AV equipment during a social engineering approach, or interfere with IR-controlled access components. Particularly useful in conference rooms and lobby environments.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect — IR capture is passive and silent; replay may cause unexpected AV or HVAC activation.
blue_team.countermeasures: Restrict IR control access to authorized personnel; use RF with rolling codes instead of IR for security-sensitive controls; monitor for unexpected AV or HVAC activation.

techniques.name: Bluetooth Reconnaissance & Attacks
techniques.description: Bluetooth scanning reveals devices in the target environment — access control readers with Bluetooth admin interfaces, printers, computers, mobile devices, and IoT sensors. Some Bluetooth-enabled access control systems have administrative interfaces vulnerable to default credential attacks or protocol weaknesses. BLE scanning also reveals the density and type of connected devices, informing network segmentation intelligence.

blue_team.detection: Bluetooth scanning visible in enterprise monitoring; unexpected BLE device appearing in scan results near access control readers.
blue_team.countermeasures: Disable Bluetooth on access control readers where not required; use encrypted BLE; monitor for unusual Bluetooth activity; WIDS with Bluetooth scanning capability.

techniques.name: Zigbee / Z-Wave Reconnaissance
techniques.description: Zigbee and Z-Wave are low-power mesh protocols used in building automation, smart locks, HVAC control, and lighting systems. Reconnaissance of these protocols can reveal building automation topology and identify smart lock installations that may be vulnerable to replay or protocol attacks. As smart building systems become more prevalent, this attack surface is growing in relevance for physical red team engagements.

blue_team.detection: Zigbee/Z-Wave scanner device near building automation equipment; unexpected commands to smart locks or HVAC.
blue_team.countermeasures: Use encrypted Zigbee (Zigbee 3.0 with AES-128); change default network keys; monitor building automation for unexpected commands; segment IoT devices from main network.

techniques.name: SDR Passive Listening
techniques.description: Software Defined Radio allows capture and analysis of arbitrary RF signals across a wide frequency range. In physical red teaming, SDR is primarily a reconnaissance and analysis tool — identifying unknown wireless systems, analyzing proprietary protocols, and supporting replay attack development against custom or unusual systems. SDR tools are not commonly deployed in standard engagements but are invaluable when encountering non-standard access control or alarm systems.

blue_team.detection: SDR hardware visible near facility; RF monitoring may detect wide-band scanning activity; difficult to detect passive listening.
blue_team.countermeasures: Encrypt all RF communications where possible; use frequency hopping; TEMPEST shielding for sensitive areas; RF monitoring for unusual signal activity near facility.

tactics.name: Social Engineering
tactics.description: The operator is trying to get people to grant access or share information.

techniques.name: Offensive Threat Modeling
techniques.description: Before committing to a social engineering or physical bypass approach, a red team operator performs threat modeling from the attacker's perspective — enumerating all viable access vectors, scoring each by probability of success and risk of detection, and selecting the optimal attack path. This involves mapping the target's security controls identified during recon against the team's available techniques, asking which approach (pure SE, pure physical, wireless-enabled SE, combined) gives the highest success probability with the lowest signature. Attack trees are the primary tool: each root node is an objective, branches are techniques, and leaves are specific actions. Offensive threat modeling is what separates a rehearsed, high-confidence engagement from improvised guesswork.

references.title: Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking
references.author: Chris Hadnagy

blue_team.detection: No direct detection — this is pre-engagement planning; OSINT activity may be detectable via web logs or LinkedIn monitoring.
blue_team.countermeasures: Monitor for unusual employee profile lookups on LinkedIn; Google dork alerts for your domain; Shodan monitoring for exposed assets; security awareness about OSINT exposure.

techniques.name: Pretexting & Scenario Building
techniques.description: A pretext is a fabricated scenario that gives you a plausible reason to be somewhere you have no legitimate right to be. Effective pretexts are built on intelligence gathered during reconnaissance — they reference real vendors the target uses, real departments that exist, real systems in maintenance. The more specific and accurate the pretext, the more resilient it is to probing questions. Scenario building involves scripting the full arc of the interaction: your opening line, your response to challenges, your behavior if pushed beyond your script, and your abort criteria.

blue_team.detection: Post-incident review may reveal inconsistencies in pretext story; employees may report suspicious conversation after the fact.
blue_team.countermeasures: Security awareness training on pretext recognition; verify all visitors through established process regardless of story; call-back verification for any unusual request; document all visitor interactions.

references.title: Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking
references.author: Chris Hadnagy

techniques.name: Elicitation
techniques.description: Elicitation is the technique of extracting information from a target through natural conversation without them realizing they are being interrogated. Unlike direct questioning, elicitation uses open-ended prompts, flattery, apparent ignorance, and deliberate incorrect statements — which people instinctively correct — to draw out sensitive information. In physical red teaming, elicitation is used to identify badge access levels, security procedures, shift schedules, vendor relationships, and system configurations.

blue_team.detection: No direct observable indicators — conversation appears natural; post-incident review of what information was shared; employee reports feeling "pumped for information" after interaction.
blue_team.countermeasures: Security awareness training focused on information-sharing in conversation; need-to-know culture; employees briefed on elicitation techniques; debrief employees after unusual visitor interactions.

references.title: Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking
references.author: Chris Hadnagy

techniques.name: Impersonation
techniques.description: Impersonation is the live execution of a pretext — presenting yourself as someone you are not in a way convincing enough to gain access, extract information, or manipulate behavior. Effective impersonation requires more than a costume: it demands appropriate body language, familiarity with the role you are playing, plausible props, and the confidence to hold the persona under pressure. High-value roles include HVAC technicians, IT support staff, fire safety inspectors, delivery drivers, and cleaning crews — roles that have legitimate reasons to access restricted areas and are rarely challenged.

blue_team.detection: Security staff challenge reveals inconsistency in story or credentials; visitor log discrepancy; camera footage shows unknown individual in restricted area without escort.
blue_team.countermeasures: Two-factor physical verification; visitor escort policy; security awareness training on credential verification; mantrap vestibules; challenge culture.

techniques.name: Costume & Prop Construction
techniques.description: Physical props and attire are the material layer of social engineering. A hi-vis vest and hard hat transforms an unknown visitor into an expected contractor. A clipboard with official-looking paperwork provides behavioral cover while moving through a facility. Props must be appropriate to the pretext, accurate enough to withstand casual inspection, and practical enough not to impede the operational objective. Prop sourcing should be done well in advance — never show up with a prop you have not practiced carrying naturally.

blue_team.detection: Security staff noticing inconsistencies in attire or props; wrong logo, incorrect uniform style, props not matching stated role; visitor log discrepancies.
blue_team.countermeasures: Security awareness training on uniform and credential verification; challenge culture; visitor escort policy; photo ID requirement for all visitors regardless of attire.

techniques.name: Tailgating & Piggybacking
techniques.description: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured door without presenting credentials. Piggybacking is the same act with the target's knowledge — they hold the door for you. Both exploit social norms around courtesy and the assumption that someone moving confidently belongs there. Effective tailgating requires timing the approach as a valid user presents credentials, an appropriate cover story if challenged, and props that justify presence. Carrying large or awkward items dramatically increases success rates.
prerequisites: Plausible reason to be at entry point established
Authorized person flow confirmed at target entry

blue_team.detection: Tailgating detection cameras; mantrap alert on multiple entries per badge read; security staff observing two people enter on one badge swipe; access log anomaly.
blue_team.countermeasures: Mantrap or airlock vestibule enforcing one-person-at-a-time entry; tailgating detection cameras with real-time alerts; security awareness training empowering employees to challenge.

techniques.name: Vishing
techniques.description: Vishing involves calling target employees and using a fabricated pretext to extract information or manipulate behavior over the phone. In physical red teaming, vishing is typically used to gather intelligence before an in-person visit — identifying security vendors, shift schedules, access procedures — or to prime a target before on-site execution by calling ahead as 'IT support' to establish a reason to be there. A burner phone or VoIP service with caller ID spoofing capability prevents attribution.

blue_team.detection: Call logs showing unusual inbound/outbound patterns; employee reports suspicious call requesting sensitive info; caller ID spoofing may show as internal or trusted number.
blue_team.countermeasures: Caller ID verification policy — never trust inbound caller ID alone; call-back verification for sensitive requests; vishing simulation training; process requiring out-of-band confirmation for credential or access requests by phone.

techniques.name: Phishing (pre-engagement support)
techniques.description: Phishing has a direct role in physical engagements as a preparatory tactic. A well-timed phishing campaign can harvest credentials for use in physical access scenarios, establish a false digital presence that supports an in-person pretext, or deliver a payload that arms a later hardware implant phase. Phishing for physical engagements is always conducted under the same written authorization as the physical work.

blue_team.detection: Email gateway alerts on suspicious links or attachments; user reports phishing email; SIEM alert on credential submission to lookalike domain; endpoint alert on payload execution.
blue_team.countermeasures: Email gateway with link scanning and sandboxing; DMARC/DKIM/SPF enforcement; phishing simulation training; MFA preventing credential replay even after successful phish; DNS filtering blocking lookalike domains.

techniques.name: Authority Exploitation
techniques.description: Authority is one of the most reliable psychological levers in social engineering. People are conditioned to comply with authority figures — inspectors, executives, IT administrators — even when those figures cannot be properly verified. Authority exploitation positions you in a role with implied or explicit authority over the target, then uses that authority to bypass normal security procedures. Confidence and specificity are the primary tools: a vague authority claim is easily challenged, while a specific and detailed one is rarely questioned.

references.title: Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking
references.author: Chris Hadnagy

blue_team.detection: Requests that bypass normal process under claimed authority; pressure to skip verification steps; unusual visitor claiming executive access.
blue_team.countermeasures: Written policy that no verbal authority overrides physical security verification; security awareness training; all visitors verified regardless of claimed seniority.

techniques.name: Urgency & Distraction
techniques.description: Urgency bypasses deliberate thinking. When a target believes a situation is time-critical — a server is down, an inspection is running behind, a fire alarm test must happen now — they are less likely to follow verification procedures and more likely to grant access immediately. Distraction techniques occupy the attention of security personnel while a confederate performs the operational objective. Both are most effective when combined with a strong pretext and authority framing.

references.title: Social Engineering: The Science of Human Hacking
references.author: Chris Hadnagy

blue_team.detection: Employee reports being pressured to bypass normal process; security staff notices rushed or agitated visitor; post-incident review reveals process was bypassed.
blue_team.countermeasures: Written policy that urgency never overrides verification; security awareness training on urgency exploitation; slow-down protocol for any request bypassing normal process.

techniques.name: Vendor & Supply Chain Impersonation
techniques.description: Many organizations grant broad physical access to third-party vendors, contractors, delivery personnel, and maintenance crews with minimal verification. Impersonating a known vendor — an IT hardware supplier, a copier service technician, a HVAC contractor — can yield escorted access to server rooms, network closets, and executive floors that standard visitor procedures would not permit. Effective execution requires OSINT to identify actual vendors the target uses (job postings, LinkedIn, dumpster diving for invoices), construction of a plausible service visit pretext, and attire and props matching the vendor's real field technicians.

tools.name: Fake work order or service ticket

blue_team.detection: Vendor not in approved vendor list; visit not pre-scheduled; inconsistencies in vendor documentation; camera footage of vendor accessing areas beyond stated scope.
blue_team.countermeasures: Approved vendor list with pre-scheduled visit policy; vendor verification process (call vendor company directly, not the number they provide); vendor escort throughout facility; access limited strictly to area of stated work; visitor log with photo ID.

tactics.name: Implants & Hardware
tactics.description: The operator is trying to place devices that give access to networks or systems.

techniques.name: HID Payload Injection
techniques.description: A USB HID attack tool emulates a keyboard when plugged into a target computer, executing a pre-programmed keystroke payload at speeds far exceeding human typing. The payload can open a terminal, download and execute code, exfiltrate credentials, create backdoor accounts, or any other action achievable via keyboard input. HID attacks are effective because USB keyboards are trusted by default in all major operating systems, and the attack completes in seconds — well within an unattended workstation window.

blue_team.detection: Endpoint DLP alert on new HID device connection; SIEM alert on USB HID registration; EDR behavioral detection for rapid keystroke injection; unusual process execution on workstation.
blue_team.countermeasures: USB device allowlisting via GPO or MDM; endpoint DLP monitoring for new HID device registration; EDR with behavioral detection for keystroke injection; disable USB ports on unattended workstations.

techniques.name: Multi-Vector HID + Network
techniques.description: The Bash Bunny combines HID attack capability with network interface emulation and mass storage in a single device. It can simultaneously emulate a keyboard, Ethernet adapter, and USB drive, enabling complex multi-stage payloads that exfiltrate data, capture credentials, and establish network persistence in a single insertion. It is the tool of choice when a single unattended workstation access window must accomplish multiple objectives.

blue_team.detection: Endpoint DLP alert on HID device; SIEM alert on new USB device; network monitoring shows new unknown device; EDR behavioral detection for keystroke injection combined with network activity.
blue_team.countermeasures: USB device allowlisting; NAC preventing unauthorized network access; EDR with behavioral detection; network segmentation; workstation auto-lock; port blockers on unattended workstations.

techniques.name: Covert USB Implant
techniques.description: The O.MG Plug appears as a normal charger or USB accessory but contains a wireless-capable HID implant. It can be remotely triggered over Wi-Fi to execute payloads, making it a persistent drop device that does not require physical retrieval to operate. Designed for long-term placement in environments where a device charging from a USB port would not raise suspicion.

blue_team.detection: Device appears as normal charger — difficult to visually distinguish; endpoint may alert on new HID or network device; wireless traffic from implant detectable.
blue_team.countermeasures: USB device allowlisting; charging-only USB ports in public areas; endpoint monitoring for new device registration; RF monitoring for implant beacon traffic.

techniques.name: Keylogger + Payload
techniques.description: The Key Croc is an inline keyboard interceptor placed between a keyboard and computer that captures keystrokes and executes DuckyScript payloads triggered by specific keywords. It passively captures credentials, commands, and sensitive input, and can activate payloads when the user types a trigger string. It is one of the most operationally precise implants for targeted credential capture on a specific workstation.

blue_team.detection: Inline device between keyboard and computer detectable by physical inspection; endpoint may alert on new HID device; captured credentials replayed from unusual location.
blue_team.countermeasures: Physical inspection of workstations — check keyboard connections; endpoint monitoring for new HID devices; use wireless keyboards (eliminates inline intercept); MFA preventing credential replay.

techniques.name: Network Implant / Backdoor
techniques.description: The LAN Turtle is a covert network implant that provides remote access to the target network by establishing an outbound tunnel. Placed inline between a computer and network port — disguised as a USB Ethernet adapter — it creates a persistent network foothold that survives reboots. It includes modules for network scanning, credential capture, and reverse shell establishment, and its outbound-only connection model avoids many perimeter firewall restrictions.

blue_team.detection: New unknown device on DHCP logs; NAC policy violation alert; unusual outbound connection from unknown MAC; C2 traffic patterns.
blue_team.countermeasures: Network Access Control (NAC); 802.1X port authentication; DHCP monitoring for unknown MACs; network segmentation; regular physical network port audits.

techniques.name: Passive Network Reconnaissance
techniques.description: The Shark Jack is a compact network implant designed for fast, passive network reconnaissance. Plugged into any network port, it automatically scans the local segment, identifies hosts, and captures network data. It is designed for short-duration deployment and rapid extraction — plug in, wait, pull out. Preferred for reliability in fixed-port deployments where power is available.
