blue_team.detection: Unknown MAC address on DHCP logs; NAC alert on unauthorized device; brief network scan activity visible in logs.
blue_team.countermeasures: NAC requiring authentication before network access; 802.1X port authentication; DHCP monitoring for unknown MACs; physical port locks on unused ports.

techniques.name: Rogue Access Point as Drop
techniques.description: A Wi-Fi Pineapple deployed as a drop device creates a persistent rogue access point inside the target environment. Placed in a concealed location with a power source, it operates autonomously — capturing credentials, performing MitM attacks on clients, and providing a Wi-Fi C2 channel back to the operator. The Enterprise version is recommended for multi-floor deployments due to improved range and higher client density handling.

blue_team.detection: WIDS detects rogue AP inside facility; clients connecting to unknown BSSID; RF scanning detects device in unusual location.
blue_team.countermeasures: WIDS with physical location correlation; 802.1X on all wired ports; regular RF sweeps of facility; physical security of network closets and ceiling spaces.

techniques.name: Wiegand Bus Implant
techniques.description: The ESPKey taps directly into the Wiegand data bus between an RFID reader and the access control panel. Wiegand is a simple, unencrypted two-wire protocol carrying card data in plaintext. The ESPKey captures every credential presented to the reader and transmits the data wirelessly. Installation requires brief access to the back of the reader or the cable run, and the device is small enough to conceal within or behind most reader housings — turning the reader itself into a persistent credential harvester.
prerequisites: Access to Wiegand reader back panel or cable run

blue_team.detection: Physical tamper evidence on reader; reader malfunction; access log shows credential enumeration; OSDP tamper detection alert.
blue_team.countermeasures: OSDP with AES-128 encryption renders Wiegand bus implants useless; reader tamper detection; sealed back-box installation; encrypted access control panel communication.

techniques.name: RFID Development Implant
techniques.description: The Doppelganger RFID Development Board is a more flexible platform for custom access control implant scenarios. It can be programmed for credential capture, emulation, or relay attacks, and its open platform allows custom firmware for specific access control system targets. It is the right tool when the ESPKey's fixed functionality is insufficient for the target environment's protocol or when a custom implant behavior is required.

blue_team.detection: Physical tamper evidence on reader; reader malfunction; access log shows credential enumeration; OSDP tamper detection alert.
blue_team.countermeasures: OSDP with AES-128 encryption renders implant useless; reader tamper detection and sealed installation; regular reader inspection; encrypted access control panel communication.

techniques.name: Device Concealment & Placement
techniques.description: A hardware implant is only as effective as its placement. Devices placed in obvious locations will be discovered during the next cleaning cycle or security sweep. Effective placement leverages environmental features — ceiling tiles, behind mounted equipment, inside cable management trays, beneath raised flooring, within junction boxes — that are infrequently accessed. If accidentally discovered, the device should appear as plausible infrastructure rather than foreign hardware.

blue_team.detection: Physical discovery during security sweep; RF emissions from device; visual inspection of unusual objects in facility.
blue_team.countermeasures: Regular physical security sweeps including ceiling spaces and utility areas; TSCM for high-security areas; RF monitoring; photograph and document all equipment in sensitive areas.

techniques.name: Power Source Selection
techniques.description: The choice between battery power and wall tap is one of the most significant operational decisions for any dropped implant. Battery-powered devices are self-contained but have finite operational lifetime. Wall-tapped devices operate indefinitely but require access to a power outlet and limit placement options. PoE-powered implants placed at network ports are a particularly elegant solution when available, as network connectivity and power arrive on the same cable.

blue_team.detection: Wall tap devices may cause electrical anomalies; USB power bank limits operational time; discovery during physical sweep.
blue_team.countermeasures: Regular physical inspection of power outlets and USB charging points; monitor for unauthorized wall tap devices; RF monitoring to detect battery-powered implants nearing end of life.

techniques.name: Covert Retrieval Planning
techniques.description: Every device placed inside a target must have a retrieval plan. Unrecovered implants are a serious liability — they can be discovered during security sweeps and create attribution risk. Retrieval plans must be developed before placement and should account for changed access conditions, increased security posture, and time windows where retrieval is feasible. A confederate retrieval option should be considered for high-risk placements.

blue_team.detection: Retrieval attempt may require re-entry — detectable through access logs; operator in restricted area without clear purpose.
blue_team.countermeasures: Access log monitoring for unusual re-entry patterns; camera coverage of areas where implants were placed; correlate physical access events with network/RF anomalies.

techniques.name: Dead Drop vs. Active Exfil
techniques.description: Hardware implants can be configured in two fundamental modes. Dead drop mode means the device passively captures data stored locally for physical retrieval — no network traffic is generated and the device is essentially invisible to network monitoring. Active exfil mode means the device is actively transmitting captured data to an operator-controlled server, which has higher real-time capability but generates detectable network activity. Most physical engagements use dead drop mode to minimize detection risk.

blue_team.detection: Dead drop mode — data only exfiltrated when device is physically retrieved, minimizing network detection; active mode generates C2 traffic detectable by network monitoring.
blue_team.countermeasures: NAC and network monitoring to detect active C2 traffic; RF monitoring for wireless exfiltration; physical security sweeps to find dead drop devices; TSCM for high-security areas.

tactics.name: Exfiltration
tactics.description: The operator is trying to collect evidence or data and get it out of the site.

techniques.name: Document & Environment Photography
techniques.description: Systematic photography of the target environment during and after entry is the primary evidence collection method in physical red team engagements. This includes capturing access control system details, sensitive documents, server room contents, network infrastructure, whiteboard contents, and any other intelligence demonstrating the scope of access achieved. Body-worn cameras provide continuous coverage without drawing attention to the documentation act.

blue_team.detection: Camera use in restricted area visible on CCTV; employee reports individual photographing sensitive materials; flash or phone screen visible.
blue_team.countermeasures: Camera-detection systems in sensitive areas; no photography policy enforced at entry; visitor escort preventing unsupervised access; screen privacy filters; clean desk policy.

techniques.name: Physical Document Removal
techniques.description: Physical removal of documents from the target facility demonstrates that sensitive material is accessible and portable. In engagements where this is in scope, items such as network diagrams, employee directories, security procedures, access control documentation, and printed credentials may be removed as evidence. All removed items must be documented, handled per the rules of engagement, and returned to the client at engagement conclusion.

blue_team.detection: Missing documents during audit; camera footage of individual removing documents; exit screening triggers.
blue_team.countermeasures: Document classification and tracking; exit screening at high-security facilities; clean-desk policy; DLP on copiers and printers.

techniques.name: Credential Harvesting On-Site
techniques.description: Physical environments are rich with credential exposure — passwords on sticky notes, whiteboards with system credentials, unlocked workstations with cached sessions, printed access lists, and network equipment with default credentials visible on labels. Systematic documentation of these exposures during physical access is a high-value deliverable that demonstrates the downstream risk of physical access beyond just the entry itself.

blue_team.detection: Camera footage of individual photographing screens or whiteboards; clean desk policy violation discovered; employee reports suspicious photography.
blue_team.countermeasures: Clean desk policy strictly enforced; screen privacy filters on monitors in open areas; whiteboard policy — sensitive info erased after use; camera detection in sensitive areas; visitor escort.

techniques.name: Badge / Card Cloning During Access
techniques.description: Once physical access is achieved, opportunities arise to clone credentials from unattended badge holders, charging docks, or staff desks. A cloned credential extends access beyond the initial entry window and enables re-entry or persistence. This is distinct from long-range skimming — this technique involves direct proximity to an unattended or briefly exposed card, which is possible once inside the facility.

blue_team.detection: Cloned credential used after engagement window; simultaneous credential use; anti-passback violation in access control logs.
blue_team.countermeasures: Anti-passback rules; credential geofencing; monitor for simultaneous credential use; DESFire EV2/EV3 with AES-128 prevents cloning.

techniques.name: USB Data Exfiltration
techniques.description: USB-based exfiltration tools copy targeted files, extract credential stores, or run automated data collection scripts from an unattended workstation. The Rubber Ducky and Bash Bunny can be programmed with payloads that identify and copy high-value files to USB storage in seconds. This technique requires brief physical access to a powered, logged-in workstation — a condition frequently met in office environments where employees step away briefly.

blue_team.detection: DLP alert on USB mass storage connection; endpoint log showing file copy to USB; EDR behavioral alert.
blue_team.countermeasures: USB mass storage device blocking via GPO/MDM; DLP monitoring for mass file copy; endpoint encryption; USB port blockers on sensitive workstations.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Capture
techniques.description: Placing a network capture device on the target LAN collects traffic that may contain plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, internal service data, and network topology information. The Shark Jack performs automated network reconnaissance and capture during short deployment windows. The LAN Turtle maintains persistent capture capability for longer engagements. Captured traffic is analyzed post-engagement for credentials and network intelligence.

blue_team.detection: Unknown device on DHCP logs; promiscuous mode detection; NAC alert on unauthorized port access.
blue_team.countermeasures: Network encryption (TLS/HTTPS everywhere); NAC preventing unknown device access; 802.1X authentication on all ports; promiscuous mode detection.

techniques.name: Wireless Credential Capture
techniques.description: Within the target facility, the wireless attack surface expands dramatically — clients connecting to internal SSIDs expose WPA2 handshakes, NTLM credentials, and session tokens not accessible from outside the perimeter. The Wi-Fi Pineapple deployed inside captures this traffic at significantly higher fidelity than external wireless attacks. Internal wireless capture is one of the highest-yield activities once initial access is achieved.

blue_team.detection: WIDS detects rogue AP or evil twin inside facility; clients connecting to unknown BSSID; endpoint alert on unrecognized network.
blue_team.countermeasures: WPA3 Enterprise with certificate-based authentication; WIDS deployed inside facility; 802.1X preventing credential capture; network segmentation limiting blast radius.

techniques.name: Screen Capture / Shoulder Surfing Documentation
techniques.description: Unlocked or unattended screens visible during physical traversal may display sensitive information — internal dashboards, HR systems, financial data, security monitoring interfaces, or active credentials. Body-worn cameras capture this incidentally during normal movement, while deliberate documentation of specific screens provides targeted evidence of data exposure risk. This technique requires no interaction with the target system and leaves no forensic trace.

blue_team.detection: Camera footage of individual photographing screens; employee reports someone looking over their shoulder; privacy filter absence noted during security walkthrough.
blue_team.countermeasures: Screen privacy filters on all workstations in open or visible areas; clean screen policy — lock when stepping away; position monitors away from public sight lines; security awareness training on shoulder surfing.

tactics.name: Persistence
tactics.description: The operator is trying to keep or regain access after the first entry.

techniques.name: Planted Hardware
techniques.description: Hardware implants left in place after the initial access phase provide ongoing access capability without requiring re-entry. The LAN Turtle provides persistent network access, the Wi-Fi Pineapple maintains a wireless foothold, and the ESPKey continues harvesting credentials indefinitely. The operational lifetime of planted hardware depends on power source, network connectivity, and the target's security sweep schedule. All planted hardware must be recovered per engagement rules of engagement.

blue_team.detection: Physical device discovery during security sweep; network anomaly from implant; WIDS detection; unusual RF emissions.
blue_team.countermeasures: Regular physical security sweeps including ceiling spaces; TSCM for high-security areas; NAC preventing implant network access; WIDS for wireless implants; audit all network ports.

techniques.name: Retained Physical Credentials
techniques.description: Cloned RFID credentials and physically duplicated keys allow re-entry to the target facility without requiring a new social engineering or bypass approach. A cloned credential can be used by any operator with the appropriate emulation device, extending the team's access capability across the full engagement window. Key bitting captured via a Lishi tool can be used to produce a functional duplicate key that provides silent, repeatable re-entry.
prerequisites: PRTF-5.06 — LF RFID Cloning or PRTF-3.11 — Lishi

blue_team.detection: Cloned credential used after engagement; anti-passback violation; access at unusual time or location post-engagement.
blue_team.countermeasures: Credential rotation after suspected compromise; anti-passback and geofencing; time-limited credentials for contractors and visitors; monitor for access outside normal patterns.

techniques.name: Backdoor Account Creation
techniques.description: A HID payload deployed on an unattended workstation can create a local or domain account, add an account to privileged groups, or modify authentication settings to allow future logical access. This technique bridges the physical and cyber domains — the physical access enables the account creation, which then provides persistent access that does not require physical re-entry. Typically the highest-impact finding in engagements that include a cyber scope component.

blue_team.detection: New local account in system logs; EDR alert on account creation; SIEM correlation with physical access event; unexpected privileged account.
blue_team.countermeasures: Privileged Access Management (PAM); SIEM monitoring for new account creation; endpoint detection of local admin creation; regular account audits; workstation auto-lock.

techniques.name: Re-entry Route Documentation
techniques.description: During the initial access phase, documenting identified entry vectors — successful techniques, bypass methods that worked, timing windows, and staff patterns — builds an operational playbook for re-entry without requiring a full recon cycle. Body-worn camera footage reviewed after the engagement reveals details not captured in field notes, and identified blind spots noted during transit become the basis for a re-entry route that avoids improved defenses.

blue_team.detection: Difficult to detect during authorized access — operator is documenting; post-engagement discovery of detailed entry route notes on seized device.
blue_team.countermeasures: Remediate all identified vulnerabilities immediately after engagement; re-test all entry points; physical security review after each red team engagement; access control audit post-engagement.

techniques.name: Covert Asset Check-In
techniques.description: Hardware implants placed during the engagement must be periodically verified as operational. The LAN Turtle and Wi-Fi Pineapple provide network-based check-in capability that the operator can monitor remotely. The ESPKey stores captured data locally and requires physical retrieval to confirm capture. Establishing a check-in cadence and a go/no-go threshold for retrieval ensures planted assets are recovered before being discovered or becoming inoperable.

blue_team.detection: Network monitoring detects periodic beacon from implant; RF sweep detects implant signal; physical discovery during post-engagement sweep.
blue_team.countermeasures: TSCM sweep after engagement; NAC detecting implant periodic check-in traffic; RF monitoring for unusual signals; thorough physical sweep of all areas accessed during engagement.
